claims.text: The patient presented with severe left knee pain and functional limitation due to end-stage osteoarthritis, characterized by a constant dull ache with episodes of sharp pain on weight-bearing, rated 8/10 to 9/10, with onset gradual over 3 years and significant worsening in the last 12 months.

Pre-operative examination revealed significant left knee deformity with valgus alignment, tenderness along the medial joint line, reduced range of motion with pain on flexion beyond 70 degrees, and mild effusion, with no signs of erythema, warmth, or active infection.

Pre-operative investigations on 20/12/25 showed mild anaemia with haemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, normal white cell count and platelets, normal urea and electrolytes, normal liver function tests, normal CRP, normal urinalysis, and a normal ECG with sinus rhythm.
The patient has no known drug or environmental allergies and no significant past medical history other than end-stage osteoarthritis of the left knee.
Family history includes a mother with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a father with hypertension, with no family history of osteoarthritis or anaesthetic complications.

Social history indicates the patient lives with parents, is independent in activities of daily living but requires assistance for prolonged walking or standing, is a non-smoker, drinks alcohol occasionally (approximately 4 units per week), and has no recreational drug use.

Pre-operative management included a prescription for ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily and dietary advice to increase iron-rich foods to address mild anaemia, with plans to re-evaluate haemoglobin levels on admission.
The patient was assessed as ASA grade I, cleared for general anaesthesia, and instructed to follow a carbohydrate loading regimen the day prior to surgery and fast from midnight.
Formal written consent for total left knee replacement was obtained on 21/12/25 after discussion of benefits, risks including infection and thromboembolism, and the anticipated 4-day hospital stay.

On admission on 05/01/26, the patient was alert and cooperative with stable vital signs (HR 74 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14 br/min, Temp 36.7°C, SpO2 98%), and the left knee showed gross deformity consistent with end-stage OA without signs of infection.

Total left knee replacement was performed on 05/01/26 under general anaesthesia, revealing severe cartilage degeneration and subchondral bone exposure, with implantation of a cemented total knee prosthesis and minimal blood loss.

Intra-operative prophylaxis included Cefuroxime 1.5g IV, and post-operative care initially included Tinzaparin 4,500 units subcutaneously once daily for thromboprophylaxis and Paracetamol 1g orally QDS PRN for pain.

Post-operative transfer to the PACU occurred at 12:15 on 05/01/26 with the patient drowsy but rousable, receiving 2L/min oxygen via nasal cannula and a PCA pump with IV morphine 2 mg for pain management.
On 05/01/26, the surgical site was clean with minimal serous drainage, no signs of infection, and the patient reported moderate pain (6/10) at rest and increased discomfort with movement.

Thromboprophylaxis was switched to Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily on 05/01/26, and pain management was updated to Paracetamol 1g every 6 hours regularly with Codeine phosphate 30 mg PRN for breakthrough pain.
Initial physiotherapy on 06/01/26 focused on gentle mobilisation, achieving 40 degrees of flexion with mild discomfort (VAS 4/10), and included deep breathing exercises with no adverse events.
On 06/01/26, the patient reported mild pain well controlled with oral analgesia, with the surgical site clean and dry, no signs of infection or DVT, and stable vital signs.
Physiotherapy on 07/01/26 involved walking a short distance with a Zimmer frame and assisted knee exercises, with the patient reporting mild discomfort (3/10) and tolerating the session well.

Occupational therapy on 07/01/26 assessed activities of daily living, noting the patient maintained good balance with verbal prompts but required guidance to protect the operated knee, leading to recommendations for a raised toilet seat and sock aid.
On 07/01/26, a pharmacist review recommended switching IV paracetamol to oral 1g QDS and continuing Ibuprofen 400mg TDS if tolerated.

On 07/01/26, the patient had mild post-operative anaemia with haemoglobin 108 g/L, and the plan included prescribing Ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily and transitioning to oral Ibuprofen 400 mg TDS for pain management.
On 08/01/26, the patient reported satisfactory pain control, was mobilising well with a Zimmer frame, and had a haemoglobin of 108 g/L with no evidence of infection or further blood loss.

Pain management on 08/01/26 was adjusted to switch regular paracetamol to PRN dosing, and discharge planning included prescribing oral Co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS for 7 days for wound infection prophylaxis.
Final physiotherapy on 08/01/26 focused on crutch use for independent mobilisation, including stair navigation, and the patient was deemed safe for discharge with crutches.
Occupational therapy on 08/01/26 confirmed the patient demonstrated independence and safety in bed transfers, crutch use, and household tasks, with recommendations for minor home adjustments.

Discharge planning on 08/01/26 included instructions for wound care, a pain management regimen of oral paracetamol 1g QDS and Ibuprofen 400mg TDS, and a follow-up appointment scheduled for 15/01/26 with the GP.
Discharge was planned for 09/01/26 with the patient to continue Ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily, Co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS for 7 days, and the prescribed pain management regimen.
